title: Aggregate and Summary Endpoints
learning_outcomes: Explain how aggregate and summary endpoints affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from counts and grouped results to a concrete API example.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on aggregate and summary endpoints in filtering, sorting, searching, and pagination. You will connect counts and grouped results to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Aggregate and Summary Endpoints matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying counts and grouped results deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Collection endpoints need explicit parameter validation, stable ordering, bounded result sizes, and predictable pagination metadata. In this lesson, treat “Aggregate and Summary Endpoints” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating aggregate and summary endpoints as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
